item.title: ARC Raiders: Ascending the Mountain Project Guide (Requirements & Rewards)
item.description:
Embark’s new project, Ascending the Mountain, is officially live in ARC Raiders until October 5, 2026. If you are trying to clear all four stages before your next Expedition departure window, you'll need to hunt down a host of materials, including elusive Sentinel Firing Cores, Sensors, and Vaporizer Regulators, which can easily turn into a brutal, multi-day grind. Here is a complete breakdown of all four stages for the Ascending the Mountain project in ARC Raiders , exactly where to speed-farm the materials, and a look at the final rewards.

ARC Raiders Phantom Targets Project Guide

Finish Phantom Targets in ARC Raiders: step-by-step tips for unreliable Pop Triggers, Blaze Grenades & Aphelion builds.

By Lucas Simons

All Ascending the Mountain Project Stages in ARC Raiders

Before taking a deep dive into the project stages, requirements, and rewards for the Ascending the Mountain project in ARC Raiders , I highly recommend writing down the total materials needed for the next two stages and farming them concurrently. Because inventory space is incredibly tight, knowing exactly what to shove into your secure container will save you from having to drop valuable loot later.

Stage 1: Research High-Altitude Mechanics

Materials

Quantity

Where to Find

Mechanical Components

10

Craft them at the Refiner, as it costs 7 Metal Parts and 3 Rubber Parts.

Can also be found in areas marked as "Mechanical" on maps.

Pop Trigger

6

Defeat Pop Arcs and scavenge their bodies.

Explosive Compound

10

Hydroponic Dome Complex on the Dam Battlegrounds map.

Headphones

2

Random apartments on the Buried City map.

Completing Stage 1 of the Ascending the Mountain project in ARC Raiders will grant players the following rewards.

  • Burletta IV Pistol
  • Extended Light Mag III Attachment
  • Silencer III Attachment

Stage 2: Begin Ignition Tests

Materials

Quantity

Where to Find

Wires

20

Get one wire for 4 seeds at Celeste​​​​​​.

Loot various electric panels or generators on the Dam Battlegrounds map, e.g., Power Generation Complex.

Voltage Converter

8

Get one Voltage Converter for 10 seeds at Celeste.

Recycle an Ion Sputter

Search Voltage Breaker Boxes and Electrical Cabinets in areas where loot is marked as "Electrical" type.

Sentinel Firing Core

2

Destroy Sentinel Arcs, commonly found around the Research & Development (R&D) building on the Dam Battlegrounds map.

Rocket Thruster

1

Assembly Workshops on the Stella Montis map.

Completing Stage 2 of the Ascending the Mountain project in ARC Raiders will grant players the following rewards.

  • Wolfpack Grenades (x2)
  • Deadline Mines (x2)
  • Trailblazer Grenades (x3)
  • Crash Mat Blueprint (x1)

Stage 3: Implement Landing Capabilities

Materials

Quantity

Where to Find

Ruined Parachute

1

Containers on the Buried City map.

Crash Mat

10

Craft Crash Mats at the Utility Station with 1x Durable Cloth and 1 Electrical Component.

Search the Tennis Court and Stacking Yard on the Riven Tides map.

Shredder Gyro

5

Destroy Shredders by visiting Stella Montis.

Breathtaking Snow Globe

3

The Grandioso Apartments and regular apartments surrounding it on the Buried City map.

Completing Stage 3 of the Ascending the Mountain project in ARC Raiders will grant players the following rewards.

  • Powered Descender (x1)
  • Raider Hatch Key (x2)
  • Rascal Launcher IV (x1)
  • Launcher Ammo (x30)

Stage 4: Final Tweaks

Materials

Quantity

Where to Find

Sensors

30

Get one sensor for 10 seeds at Celeste​​​​​​.

Search the server racks at Pilgrim's Peak on The Blue Gate and Launch Towers on Spaceport maps.

Broken Guidance System

3

Search red lockers in Hydroponic Dome Complex on the Dam Battlegrounds map.

Advanced Electrical Components

15

Craft the Advanced Electrical Components at the Refiner for 3x Wires and 2x Electrical Components.

Search the ARC Probes that randomly spawn on maps.

Vaporizer Regulator

3

Destroy Vaporizers that commonly spawn on the Riven Tides map, or during the Close Scrutiny event.

Completing Stage 4 of the Ascending the Mountain project in ARC Raiders will grant players the following rewards.

  • Hot Air Balloon Backpack Charm (x1)
  • Tactical MK3 (Defensive) Augment (x1)
  • Tempest Assault Rifle IV (x1)
  • Kinetic Converter Attachment (x1)
10 /10

item.title: Life Is Strange Developer Facing Dire Financial Situation
item.description:
The original developer of Life is Strange , Don't Nod Entertainment, is reportedly facing a dire financial situation that will likely change the studio dramatically. Despite the studio having a number of successes over the last decade, unfortunately, things aren't looking good for the Life is Strange creator right now.

Don't Nod Entertainment has produced some significant hits, but its most recent games have seen difficulties. Lost Records: Bloom and Rage was released in 2025, and saw fairly positive reviews overall, but by October, Don't Nod stated that the game had underperformed. Its most recent, Aphelion , released in 2026, received mixed reviews from critics and struggled considerably, seeing a concurrent user peak on Steam of just 219 people.

Surprise New Life is Strange: Reunion Release Officially Available Now

Fans of Life is Strange: Reunion are being treated to a brand new prequel focused on Chloe Price.

By Joshua Duckworth

Financial Report Has Worrying Outlook for Don't Nod's Future

In a financial update report from Don't Nod, the studio responsible for starting the award-winning Life is Strange franchise, explained its current situation for the first half of 2026, and how it plans to try and cope with the recent problems it's faced. Don't Nod states that for the H1 of 2026, the studio saw a 56% decline year-over-year with a revenue of €6.1 million, or just under $7.1 million USD. While Don't Nod has already taken steps to try and be competitive, it has struggled to do so, and has now unveiled a business model that could mean up to 90 of its staff will be laid off. The report states that between current economic conditions and the state of the video game industry, plus "the deterioration of Don't Nod's key financial indicators," this is a necessary step in order to try and keep its doors open and producing games. It also indicated that the studio needs to secure external financing, and that there is uncertainty whether the studio can keep its doors open past January 31, 2027, without it.

The new plan has already been approved by Don't Nod's board of directors, and negotiations have reportedly begun with union employees. These changes will see Don't Nod considerably change its business, with a plan set to focus its operations around a single production line exclusively in France, the studio's home country. The new system will bring together "the expertise required to launch new projects before the completion of current productions." The hope is that by minimizing its team size, reallocating resources, and improving efficiency, the studio will survive long enough to bring new games to the table, which would help it to rebound financially, providing the games are successful on the market.

Fans of Don't Nod and Life is Strange may recall that this isn't the first time that the studio has discussed its financial troubles in recent history. Back in June, it was revealed that Don't Nod was in danger of running out of funding entirely by November. The timing of this newly-announced financial plan and business shift is being made now to avoid that from coming to pass. Unfortunately, major shareholder Tencent has declined to provide further financial support or to increase its stake in the developer, further adding to Don't Nod's problems.

Providing that the plan works as intended, more news regarding Don't Nod's future releases will likely arrive in the near future, especially given its current concerns regarding continuing the business post-January 2027. With the entire game industry shaken up in recent times, it remains to be seen if Don't Nod will survive or is ultimately added to the list of many game development studios that have shut down permanently.

Source: Don't Nod

item.title: New Stardew Valley Meets Stranger Things RPG on Steam Is a Nightmare I Didn't Want to End
item.description:
There are some games I play where I know almost immediately what kind of experience I'm in for, and then there are games like Welcome to Elderfield , where I spent a good portion of its demo wondering what in the world I had gotten myself into. The cozy horror RPG from developer Chris Cote and publisher Kwalee launches on Steam on September 10, 2026, and while I can absolutely see the Stardew Valley inspiration in much of what it does, Elderfield itself feels like it belongs somewhere far stranger. In fact, after spending a few hours with the demo, I'm still not entirely sure what I experienced, only that I had a surprisingly hard time putting it down.

Part of that comes from the fact that Welcome to Elderfield takes the familiar idea of moving into a small town and turns the whole thing into something that feels like it fell straight out of an '80s horror movie. I have a farm to take care of, and much like I would in Stardew Valley , I can spend time getting to know the people who live nearby. But there is something deeply wrong with this place, and the further I got into the Steam demo, the clearer that became. With Welcome to Elderfield launching on September 10, I'm actually glad the full release is so close, because the demo ended with me wanting to know a lot more about whatever in the world is going on here.

New Stardew Valley Meets Undertale Life Sim on Steam Went Somewhere I Never Saw Coming

This new life sim on Steam blends Stardew Valley's cozy charm with Undertale's stranger side, and its demo goes somewhere I never expected.

By Josh Cotts

Welcome to Elderfield Is Delightfully, Uncomfortably Weird

Check out Welcome to Elderfield on Steam

More than anything else, Welcome to Elderfield is weird. Incredibly, delightfully weird. I wouldn't necessarily call it scary, although I'm sure some people are going to find it frightening, especially once they start running into some of the more disturbing things Elderfield has hiding around town. For me, though, it was much more unsettling than anything else, almost like one of those dreams where nothing is overtly terrifying, but everything feels wrong. My time with the Welcome to Elderfield demo was nothing short of a nightmare that I, for some reason, just didn't want to end.

Wishlist Today

The horror RPG's atmosphere has a lot to do with that, and it's probably my favorite thing about the game so far. Elderfield looks like this strange little town ripped straight out of the '80s, and once night falls, its streets take on this dim orange glow that I absolutely love. There's something strangely satisfying about hopping on my bike after dark and riding through town while that orange light washes over everything, especially when the occasional "ding" from my bike's bell breaks through the quiet. It's just eerie enough, just unsettling enough, to be almost cozy, simply because of how nostalgic it is.

More than anything else, Welcome to Elderfield is weird. Incredibly, delightfully weird.

Then there are the people who actually live in Elderfield, and somehow, they make the town even stranger. Almost everyone I met had something at least a little off about them, but the kids were somehow the weirdest of them all. One of them sent me into the local mall to "bop a Shopper on the head," which initially just straight up weirded me out. The thought of a kid telling me to beat a human being was strange, but once I actually showed up to the mall, I learned that the Shopper this kid was referring to was actually a monstrous creature that I had zero issues with bopping on the head.

But there were plenty of things off about the adults as well. For example, I spoke with an old man who wanted me to turn his coat rack into a wife because he thought it might cure his loneliness. How would I do that except find some literal sticks and stones around town to make the coat rack sort of resemble a wife that this lonely man could spend the rest of his life with, of course. I mean... tell me you've encountered something stranger than that in a game like Stardew Valley . That's right. You can't.

But it's encounters like these that ultimately had me enthralled with Welcome to Elderfield , because they really sell the world. It isn't littered with jump scares just to remind me that it's a horror game. Instead, there's just this underlying sense that the town has been operating according to its own rules for a very long time, and I'm the one who showed up without knowing any of them. Even when nothing especially disturbing was happening, I still found myself wondering what I was going to stumble across next. It's quite literally the recipe for a bad dream.

Welcome to Elderfield Has a Lot More Going On Than Farming

As strange as Elderfield is, though, there is still a fairly traditional farming sim underneath all of it. The farm itself works about how I expected it to at first, as I can till the soil before planting crops and then water them as they grow. Of course, this being Welcome to Elderfield , it doesn't take long for that side of the game to get weird either, because some of the things I can eventually grow include teeth and eyeballs. There are also tentacles that can show up around the farm, so even one of the game's most Stardew Valley -like elements doesn't get to stay normal for very long.

The Stardew Valley similarities continue once I start getting to know the people who live in town. Talking to villagers improves my relationship with them over time, and I can give them gifts to help with that as well. Some of those relationships can eventually become romantic in the full game, with marriage also being possible, so there is clearly a much larger social side to Welcome to Elderfield than what I was able to see in the demo.

More importantly, for my time with it, talking to everyone also gave me plenty to do around Elderfield. Different villagers would tell me what they needed and then send me off to take care of it, and those requests generally revolved around whatever else I was already doing in the game. Farmer Hans, for instance, gave me requests involving the farm, while Molly had me looking for materials in the mines. Other quests took me somewhere completely different, which is how I eventually ended up heading into the mall to take care of a creature called a Shopper for one of the kids in town.

Welcome to Elderfield Turns Its Mall Into a Full-Blown RPG Dungeon

And speaking of the mall, that's where Welcome to Elderfield started showing me how much further it was willing to go beyond the usual farming sim formula. The mall essentially functions as a dungeon in the demo, and once I started making my way through it, I was suddenly dealing with turn-based combat rather than simply spending another day around town (though the tutorial at the beginning of the demo had me to do a turn-based battle to learn the mechanics). Battles use action points, which determine how much I can do during my turn, so there's at least some strategy involved in deciding how I want to approach each encounter.

The RPG systems surrounding combat make some of the things I do outside of battle more important as well. Food, for example, can provide buffs that help during combat, so cooking has a practical use beyond being another activity I can spend time on. Equipment also matters once I'm heading somewhere dangerous, which means exploring Elderfield and gathering what I need along the way can directly affect how prepared I am when a fight starts.

As strange as Elderfield is, though, there is still a fairly traditional farming sim underneath all of it.

And that's undoubtedly the biggest difference between Welcome to Elderfield and something like Stardew Valley . There are obviously plenty of familiar ideas here, especially around the farm and the relationships I can build with people in town, but the RPG side gives me a different form of progression to pursue. I might start out doing something completely ordinary and then eventually find myself in a turn-based battle against something that absolutely does not belong in a farming sim, and after everything else I saw in Elderfield, that somehow stopped feeling unusual.

I Didn't Want Welcome to Elderfield's Demo to End

By the time the Welcome to Elderfield demo ended, it felt like I had only just gotten past the point where the game was introducing itself to me. I understood the basic routine by then, but I was also beginning to see how much more there was to it once the RPG side started opening up. That's what made the ending so frustrating, because I wasn't ready to stop. If anything, I felt like the demo had finally reached the point where I wanted to start digging deeper into everything it had spent the previous few hours setting up.

That's also why I'm curious to see how all of this holds up across the full game. Welcome to Elderfield is already doing enough differently to separate itself from the countless other farming sims on Steam, but a demo only has so much room to show how far those ideas can actually go. The turn-based combat, in particular, has plenty of room to become more involved once better equipment and tougher enemies enter the picture, and I'm interested to see whether the rest of the game continues finding ways to push its farming sim foundation in unexpected directions.

New Stardew Valley Meets How to Train Your Dragon Game on Steam Left Me Hungry for More
New Game Like Stardew Valley Already Has My Money, But Not Because It's Cozy
New Cozy Game Took 10 Minutes to Prove Stardew Valley Doesn't Define the Genre

Still, the fact that I was disappointed when the demo ended probably says more than anything else I could about my time with it. I went into Welcome to Elderfield mostly curious about its strange combination of genres, but I came out of the demo wishing I could have kept playing. Thankfully, with the full release right around the corner, I won't have to wonder about the rest of Elderfield for much longer.

In fact, after spending a few hours with the demo, I'm still not entirely sure what I experienced, only that I had a surprisingly hard time putting it down.

Part of that comes from the fact that Welcome to Elderfield takes the familiar idea of moving into a small town and turns the whole thing into something that feels like it fell straight out of an '80s horror movie. I have a farm to take care of, and much like I would in Stardew Valley , I can spend time getting to know the people who live nearby. But there is something deeply wrong with this place, and the further I got into the Steam demo, the clearer that became. With Welcome to Elderfield launching on September 10, I'm actually glad the full release is so close, because the demo ended with me wanting to know a lot more about whatever in the world is going on here.

New Stardew Valley Meets Undertale Life Sim on Steam Went Somewhere I Never Saw Coming

This new life sim on Steam blends Stardew Valley's cozy charm with Undertale's stranger side, and its demo goes somewhere I never expected.

By Josh Cotts

Welcome to Elderfield Is Delightfully, Uncomfortably Weird

Check out Welcome to Elderfield on Steam

More than anything else, Welcome to Elderfield is weird. Incredibly, delightfully weird. I wouldn't necessarily call it scary, although I'm sure some people are going to find it frightening, especially once they start running into some of the more disturbing things Elderfield has hiding around town. For me, though, it was much more unsettling than anything else, almost like one of those dreams where nothing is overtly terrifying, but everything feels wrong. My time with the Welcome to Elderfield demo was nothing short of a nightmare that I, for some reason, just didn't want to end.

Wishlist Today

The horror RPG's atmosphere has a lot to do with that, and it's probably my favorite thing about the game so far. Elderfield looks like this strange little town ripped straight out of the '80s, and once night falls, its streets take on this dim orange glow that I absolutely love. There's something strangely satisfying about hopping on my bike after dark and riding through town while that orange light washes over everything, especially when the occasional "ding" from my bike's bell breaks through the quiet. It's just eerie enough, just unsettling enough, to be almost cozy, simply because of how nostalgic it is.

More than anything else, Welcome to Elderfield is weird. Incredibly, delightfully weird.

Then there are the people who actually live in Elderfield, and somehow, they make the town even stranger. Almost everyone I met had something at least a little off about them, but the kids were somehow the weirdest of them all. One of them sent me into the local mall to "bop a Shopper on the head," which initially just straight up weirded me out. The thought of a kid telling me to beat a human being was strange, but once I actually showed up to the mall, I learned that the Shopper this kid was referring to was actually a monstrous creature that I had zero issues with bopping on the head.

But there were plenty of things off about the adults as well. For example, I spoke with an old man who wanted me to turn his coat rack into a wife because he thought it might cure his loneliness. How would I do that except find some literal sticks and stones around town to make the coat rack sort of resemble a wife that this lonely man could spend the rest of his life with, of course. I mean... tell me you've encountered something stranger than that in a game like Stardew Valley . That's right. You can't.

But it's encounters like these that ultimately had me enthralled with Welcome to Elderfield , because they really sell the world. It isn't littered with jump scares just to remind me that it's a horror game. Instead, there's just this underlying sense that the town has been operating according to its own rules for a very long time, and I'm the one who showed up without knowing any of them. Even when nothing especially disturbing was happening, I still found myself wondering what I was going to stumble across next. It's quite literally the recipe for a bad dream.

Welcome to Elderfield Has a Lot More Going On Than Farming

As strange as Elderfield is, though, there is still a fairly traditional farming sim underneath all of it. The farm itself works about how I expected it to at first, as I can till the soil before planting crops and then water them as they grow. Of course, this being Welcome to Elderfield , it doesn't take long for that side of the game to get weird either, because some of the things I can eventually grow include teeth and eyeballs. There are also tentacles that can show up around the farm, so even one of the game's most Stardew Valley -like elements doesn't get to stay normal for very long.

The Stardew Valley similarities continue once I start getting to know the people who live in town. Talking to villagers improves my relationship with them over time, and I can give them gifts to help with that as well. Some of those relationships can eventually become romantic in the full game, with marriage also being possible, so there is clearly a much larger social side to Welcome to Elderfield than what I was able to see in the demo.

More importantly, for my time with it, talking to everyone also gave me plenty to do around Elderfield. Different villagers would tell me what they needed and then send me off to take care of it, and those requests generally revolved around whatever else I was already doing in the game. Farmer Hans, for instance, gave me requests involving the farm, while Molly had me looking for materials in the mines. Other quests took me somewhere completely different, which is how I eventually ended up heading into the mall to take care of a creature called a Shopper for one of the kids in town.

Welcome to Elderfield Turns Its Mall Into a Full-Blown RPG Dungeon

And speaking of the mall, that's where Welcome to Elderfield started showing me how much further it was willing to go beyond the usual farming sim formula. The mall essentially functions as a dungeon in the demo, and once I started making my way through it, I was suddenly dealing with turn-based combat rather than simply spending another day around town (though the tutorial at the beginning of the demo had me to do a turn-based battle to learn the mechanics). Battles use action points, which determine how much I can do during my turn, so there's at least some strategy involved in deciding how I want to approach each encounter.

The RPG systems surrounding combat make some of the things I do outside of battle more important as well. Food, for example, can provide buffs that help during combat, so cooking has a practical use beyond being another activity I can spend time on. Equipment also matters once I'm heading somewhere dangerous, which means exploring Elderfield and gathering what I need along the way can directly affect how prepared I am when a fight starts.

As strange as Elderfield is, though, there is still a fairly traditional farming sim underneath all of it.

And that's undoubtedly the biggest difference between Welcome to Elderfield and something like Stardew Valley . There are obviously plenty of familiar ideas here, especially around the farm and the relationships I can build with people in town, but the RPG side gives me a different form of progression to pursue. I might start out doing something completely ordinary and then eventually find myself in a turn-based battle against something that absolutely does not belong in a farming sim, and after everything else I saw in Elderfield, that somehow stopped feeling unusual.

I Didn't Want Welcome to Elderfield's Demo to End

By the time the Welcome to Elderfield demo ended, it felt like I had only just gotten past the point where the game was introducing itself to me. I understood the basic routine by then, but I was also beginning to see how much more there was to it once the RPG side started opening up. That's what made the ending so frustrating, because I wasn't ready to stop. If anything, I felt like the demo had finally reached the point where I wanted to start digging deeper into everything it had spent the previous few hours setting up.

That's also why I'm curious to see how all of this holds up across the full game. Welcome to Elderfield is already doing enough differently to separate itself from the countless other farming sims on Steam, but a demo only has so much room to show how far those ideas can actually go. The turn-based combat, in particular, has plenty of room to become more involved once better equipment and tougher enemies enter the picture, and I'm interested to see whether the rest of the game continues finding ways to push its farming sim foundation in unexpected directions.

New Stardew Valley Meets How to Train Your Dragon Game on Steam Left Me Hungry for More
New Game Like Stardew Valley Already Has My Money, But Not Because It's Cozy
New Cozy Game Took 10 Minutes to Prove Stardew Valley Doesn't Define the Genre

Still, the fact that I was disappointed when the demo ended probably says more than anything else I could about my time with it. I went into Welcome to Elderfield mostly curious about its strange combination of genres, but I came out of the demo wishing I could have kept playing. Thankfully, with the full release right around the corner, I won't have to wonder about the rest of Elderfield for much longer.

item.title: It's Finally The End of an Era for Pokemon Thanks to New Release
item.description:
Pokemon Unite has finally ended a long era with a brand-new release, adding Morpeko to the game for the first time. Though 2026 is the 30th anniversary of the Pokemon franchise, it brought sad news for Pokemon Unite fans, as the game will no longer be supported at the World Championships after this year. The game was part of the World Championships 2026, but the finals before the closing ceremony were a bittersweet moment for fans and casters alike. Still, the game will keep on being actively supported, and it may be in a much better state after September and October 2026.

Pokemon Unite gave away free rewards for its anniversary this year, alongside a long event with four Legendary Pokemon making their debut. Despite the game adding almost 20 new Pokemon this year alone, some roles remain quite underrepresented, to the point that only a small part of the roster makes up for them. For example, the All-Rounder role is taken up by 35 Pokemon on the roster, and another 27 are Attackers. Instead, only 13 are Defenders, and even fewer are Speedsters. Luckily, Morpeko fixes that.

The 30 Best Electric Pokemon, Ranked

The Pokemon games let you catch tons of unique Electric-types. If you're looking for the best of the bunch, these should prove useful.

By Ben Painter

Pokemon Unite Officially Adds New Speedster After 7 Months

Pokemon Unite 's Morpeko is only the second Speedster of the year, coming seven months after the last, which was Meowth on January 9, 2026. Although Pokemon Unite is considered one of the best MOBAs to play on mobile, it has a more diverse cast in terms of actual Pokemon than roles. Morpeko is only the 12th Speedster overall, with its most recent predecessors being Meowth (2026), Galarian Rapidash (2025), and then Meowscarada (2023). The role rarely gets new additions, and it was almost two full years between Meowscarada and Galarian Rapidash. Luckily, not only is Morpeko a new Speedster, but it will be followed by Jolteon in October 2026 as another Speedster.

Pokemon Unite 's Galarian Rapidash is a Ranged Speedster, and it's the only one of its kind. As such, while Morpeko is a welcome addition to the roster for Speedster fans, it's yet another melee Pokemon, and Jolteon will follow suit. Even within the least represented roles, there can be some issues, and it's clear now that fans will have to wait quite some time before another ranged Speedster is added to the game, considering the long spans of time between each Speedster and the fact that all three Speedsters in 2026 are ranged. Still, Morpeko is a fun addition because it features its iconic Full Belly vs. Hangry form mode, giving players another tool to control the critter in battle. Its Hungry Supercharge Wheel move is also similar to its signature move from Gen 8, Aura Wheel, having different effects based on its form when used.

item.title: GTA Online Is Finally Showing Why More Games Should Embrace Mod Communities
item.description:
GTA Online has thrived for well over a decade now, and in many ways, Rockstar has the modding and roleplay community to thank. For 13 years, GTA Online has maintained a wildly impressive player base when other live-service games have come and gone. Even Rockstar's other live-service offering, Red Dead Online , hasn't thrived as much as GTA Online . Red Dead Redemption 2 's online counterpart still attracts players, but it isn't on the scale that GTA Online is. The game is simply a different beast.

The GTA Online mod and roleplay community has evolved into a massive online club, and one of the most popular servers over the years has been nopixel. Nopixel is a dedicated custom-made roleplaying server that has strictly enforced rules where every player has to stay in character. Players who want to move away from the public nopixel servers and wish to access the top-tier private servers even have to fill out an application and pay dues. That alone shows what a huge deal nopixel is, but it recently reached new heights, because Rockstar has officially partnered with the team to create nopixel V .

10 Details You Probably Missed in the GTA 6 Extended Look

GTA 6’s Extended Look was packed with small details, hidden mechanics, and easy-to-miss moments that reveal even more about Leonida.

By Josh Cotts

Rockstar Partnering With Nopixel Is Giving Mod and Roleplay Communities the Respect and Recognition They Deserve

If it wasn't for groups like nopixel, it's possible that GTA Online wouldn't have the hold that it still does. Even if modding and online roleplaying isn't your particular cup of tea, it's hard to not be impressed by the dedication that these communities have towards specific games. Nopixel has basically become its very own ongoing series set inside GTA 5 's Los Santos. When announcing nopixel V, Rockstar teased that "fan-favorite characters" would be returning. The fact that nopixel has given rise to an online world where people are being drawn to characters like it's a TV show or movie is wild and shows just how far the community has expanded GTA Online 's capabilities.

Nopixel, and the soon-to-be-released nopixel V, are great examples of how players are the true backbone of a game's success. GTA Online 's grip on gaming could have easily dwindled over time. There have been plenty of fun online games that have launched since 2013 that have had the potential to dethrone GTA Online , but many players have decided to stick around and create an even more detailed world within a world.

A Sneak Peek at What Nopixel V Will Have to Offer

  • A completely rebuilt character customization system.
  • Overhauls to buildings and neighborhoods like Downtown and Cypress Flats.
  • Over 1,000 properties for players to own.
  • The Pixel Tower is now fully enterable and features a casino, underground parking, offices, and even a nightclub.
  • New locations like fresh restaurants and a brand-new city jail.
  • Rebuilt UI

There are a lot of reasons to be excited about nopixel V, but one of the highlights of these confirmed upgrades is the character customization overhaul. Rockstar's crime-fueled title has stood the test of time, but GTA 5 's character creator is rough. Because of the Heritage System, it's really hard to make a character look how you want them to, so it's going to be interesting to see how nopixel V's rework of the custom character mechanics changes the experience.

Nopixel V isn't the only example of how GTA Online has expanded beyond its originally intended gameplay. Last year, the Grand Theft Hamlet movie hit theaters and was met with critical acclaim. Grand Theft Hamlet is a documentary about two friends, out-of-work actors Sam and Mark, who are searching for meaning during the COVID-19 lockdowns. This inspired them to film an adaptation of Hamlet entirely in GTA Online .

Between the changes to UI, new buildings and properties, and the character customization changes, nopixel V is practically GTA Online 2.0 with a roleplay-focused twist. With gamers waiting to hear from Rockstar about GTA 6 Online details, the timing makes nopixel V's upcoming debut that much more intriguing.

Rockstar and Nopixel V's Collaboration Could Mark a New Era for Modding and Roleplaying

Rockstar appreciating nopixel's dedication enough to team up with the group in an official capacity will hopefully inspire other developers to do the same. Of course, not every mod or roleplay group can be recognized this way, but communities like nopixel should get recognition for being the ultimate super fans. GTA 6 's extended look was already exciting enough and has taken over online discourse, so it says a lot that Rockstar was willing to follow that huge news up with the nopixel V announcement.

It's important to note that Rockstar isn't the only developer that has recognized its modding community in a significant way. Bethesda's Creations is the company's official online mod storefront. Modders can apply to become recognized as a Verified Creator, which allows them to make royalties off other players purchasing their work.

Here Is When Nopixel V Goes Live

  • The nopixel V closed beta is set to go live on September 8 .
  • This closed beta is invite-only.
  • Only content creators will be included in the invites.
  • The closed beta will still be live-streamed across online platforms.

Nopixel fans might not be able to jump into nopixel V right away, but it's going to be fascinating to see what the closed beta participants get up to during the live stream. This modding group has been present in the GTA Online community as far back as 2016, but the past few years have seen nopixel really hit a new level of popularity. The nopixel V closed beta is simply the next big step for the community, and it's incredibly impressive to see how something that started off as simple as a small role-playing group can boom into something that is fully recognized by the game's developer.

Why GTA 6 Will Be Rockstar's Last Traditional Sequel
Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 May Be the One Game GTA 6 Can't Touch
The Elder Scrolls 6 Is About to Take Over GTA 6's Longest-Running Meme
Nintendo Is About to Face One of the Hardest Problems With Remaking N64 Games

Now, one of the big questions is whether GTA 6 's launch will have a heavy impact on the nopixel V community or not. GTA 6 is expected to overshadow the industry for a while, so it wouldn't be surprising if a lot of nopixel V participants pivoted to the new game, especially once the online mode hits the scene. Only time will tell, but considering how dedicated the group has been for so long, I could see nopixel V thriving for many more years.
